extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century readers interested in manners, morals, and wit)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, moralising satirical essays and conduct pieces in the style of The Spectator: witty moral observation about manners, social behaviour, and taste, often using fable, dream, or letter forms. Advice focuses on tone, audience-adaptation, and didactic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral clarity / expose the vanity of men's wishes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vanity of Mens Wishes ... are sufficiently exposed by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fables or allegory (e.g., the Trap-Door and petitions to Jupiter) to reveal and censure human follies — particularly vain or extravagant desires. The moral should be explicit enough to deserve attention (the author references Socrates, Plato, Juvenal, Persius as exemplars). Anti-pattern: a fable that is merely entertaining without a discernible moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use set forms to restrain extravagant petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: By this means the Folly and Extravagance of Mens Desires may be kept within due Bounds, and not break out in absurd and ridiculous Petitions on so great and solemn an Occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing devotional or formal subjects in prose or satire, present or recommend structured/formal practices (e.g., set forms of prayer) as a device to curb ridiculous excesses. As a rhetorical device, advocating formality can itself be used to satirize impulsive desires. Example: recommending fixed prayers to prevent absurd petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting wit become malicious
rubrics_metrics.description: To turn the Discourse, which from being witty grew to be malicious, the Matron ... took occasion ... to wish that there were ... such faithful Monitors to dress the Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep humorous observation playful rather than spiteful: if a conversation or essay drifts from wit into malice, redirect toward corrective, humane satire (e.g., transform malicious gossip into a moral or imaginative conceit). Anti-pattern: humour that targets individuals with cruelty rather than correcting folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personified devices (mirror/fable/dream) to reflect truthfully
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sincere Friend were miraculously changed into a Looking-Glass, she should not be ashamed to ask its Advice very often ... The Looking-Glass ... was heretofore a Man, even I, the unfortunate Fidelio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ personified objects, dreams, or fictive transformations (a looking-glass that speaks, a dream narrative) to produce a detached, witty vantage point that permits blunt truth-telling. Example: the mirror-speaker who candidly describes the ladies' vanities gives license for truthful satire while maintaining imaginative distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value truthfulness/sincerity over flattering politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Dying, I preserv'd my Sincerity, and expressed the Truth, tho' in broken Words ... I immediately lost the Figure of a Man, and became smooth, polished, and bright, and to this day am the first Favourite of the Ladies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize frank, sincere observation even when it offends; honesty in depiction is a moral and aesthetic virtue in these essays. Flattery may win short-term favour but truthful depiction (even harsh) is ultimately more honorable and valuable as a satirical device. Anti-pattern: pandering or insincere praise to please an audience at the expense of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevate natural/pleasant imagery into moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: I would have my Readers endeavour to moralize this natural Pleasure of the Soul, and to improve this vernal Delight ... into a Christian Virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When celebrating nature or pleasurable sensations in prose, connect sensory delight to higher moral or religious lessons (e.g., gratitude, praise). Use description of landscape, seasons, birds, and brooks not merely for ornament but as a springboard to exhortation and moral reflection. Anti-pattern: purely descriptive naturalism without moral outcome when the piece intends edification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt rhetoric to the audience's valued qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: You need no more than to discover what a Man values himself for; then of all things admire that Quality ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To persuade or gain influence (in essays or depicted social manoeuvres), identify and praise the specific qualities your audience prizes; tailor examples, tone, and compliments accordingly. For writers this translates into choosing references, registers, and targets that resonate with readers' self-regard. Anti-pattern: generic praise or mismatched appeals that fail to engage the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate flattery—avoid obvious obsequiousness before superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: A great Man of common Sense must look with secret Indignation or bridled Laughter, on all the Slaves who stand round him with ready Faces to approve and smile at all he says in the gross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting courtship, patronage, or social climbing, show subtlety: overdone, transparent flattery will be read as slavish and provoke contempt. Satirical characterization should reveal the ugliness of obsequiousness rather than endorse it. Example: a secretary who flatters a Latin-using king will be exposed as ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat material or social 'gifts' as rhetorical/political instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The most prevailing way is, by what better-bred People call a Present, the Vulgar a Bribe ... Generous Wines do every Day prevail ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and portray the role of presents, entertainments, or favors as legitimate social tools for influence; in moral essays these can be shown as persuasive devices that corrupt or smooth business. Use them as concrete examples when satirising corruption or patronage. Anti-pattern: pretending material influence does not affect social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use puns and light devices sparingly and in proper context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monopoly of Punns ... has been an immemorial Privilege ... this humbler Exercise may be as instrumental in diverting us from any innovating Schemes and Hypothesis in Wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punning and light verbal games can be an innocent, social diversion and a relief within learned or tense contexts, but overuse signals poverty of thought and invites censure. Employ wordplay where it suits the company and purpose (diversion, conviviality) and avoid letting it dominate serious argument. Anti-pattern: constant punning that replaces substantive critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider local culture and social setting when choosing humorous devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The delicate Spirits among us ... sip Tea, and put up for Critic and Amour, profess likewise an equal Abhorrency for Punning ... the Atmosphere of the Kitchen ... predominates ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that styles of wit (punning, quibbling, catch-songs) have social loci and audiences: what amuses one college, kitchen-circle, or social rank may repel another. Match forms of humour to the milieu you are addressing and use characters/settings to make that contrast vivid. Anti-pattern: assuming a single comic device works across all social contexts.
